criterion_notes.c1: Examines household drinking-water service access, network supply intermittency, rationing, reliance on public cisterns/tanks and informal water markets, and household storage in small cities in Paraíba, Brazil.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, the study does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation or tenure rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure); instead, its focal exposure is generic large-scale water infrastructure project delivery (arrival of inter-basin water transfer via the São Francisco River Integration Project, PISF) alongside demographic, climatic, hydrological, and physical infrastructure factors in a DPSIR model (Table 1). Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it also fails because legal, institutional, and governance issues (e.g., weak governance, poor urban planning, master plans, water user associations, and discrepancies with official ANA/SINISA indicators) appear only as unanalysed macro-governance background commentary and policy recommendations rather than an empirically examined governance or institutional exposure.
criterion_notes.c3: Multi-method empirical study integrating primary household questionnaires (n = 413 across 2021 and 2024) with secondary geospatial (MapBiomas) and official statistical/hydrological data (IBGE, ANA, AESA, SNIS, SGB).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete household access, continuity/reliability, and affordability outcomes, including weekly water shortage prevalence (79% in 2021; 69.08% in 2024), days without tap water per week/month, non-networked urban households, and informal water market purchases and expenditures as a share of the minimum wage.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (413 surveyed households in small municipalities in Paraíba, plus municipal-level secondary data across 21 municipalities), exposure (implementation/water arrival of the PISF inter-basin transfer infrastructure and DPSIR physical/demographic drivers), outcomes (supply intermittency, coping sources, informal water purchases, municipal agricultural/industrial trends), and study design (multi-method DPSIR case study with repeated cross-sectional surveys and longitudinal secondary data) are clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Published in English, an eligible review language without translation.

evidence_quotes.quote: This study assesses water security challenges in small municipalities of Paraíba, Brazil, analyzing local impacts of the São Francisco River Integration Project (PISF).

In 2024, despite increased reservoir storage, 69.08% of households reported weekly water shortages. Communities coped through cisterns, informal markets, and public water sources, disproportionately affecting low-income groups and amplifying social inequalities.
Thus, this study analyses water security in small semiarid municipalities, assessing the impacts of the arrival of the São Francisco River Integration Project (PISF) waters on local populations.
The questionnaire was applied in 2021 and 2024 to compare stakeholders’ answers and assess the PISF impacts.

Although frequently attributed to water scarcity, the supply intermittency observed in the municipalities analyzed is strongly linked to weak governance, poor urban planning, inadequate infrastructure, and spatial inequality in service distribution (Cordão et al. 2020; Grasham et al. 2022).

raw_response.exposure: Arrival and infrastructure implementation of the São Francisco River Integration Project (PISF) inter-basin water transfer alongside biophysical, demographic, and physical distribution infrastructure factors in the DPSIR framework
raw_response.outcome: Household water supply intermittency and weekly shortages, days without tap water, reliance on cisterns and informal water markets, household water purchase cost relative to minimum wage, and municipal agricultural, livestock, and industrial growth
raw_response.population_and_sample: Households/residents in small municipalities of Paraíba, Brazil served by the Poções-Epitácio Pessoa Water System (n = 413 household questionnaires: 154 in 2021 and 259 in 2024; abstract notes five municipalities while Methods specifies four representative small cities: Pocinhos, Cabaceiras, Pedra Lavrada, and Boa Vista), plus municipal-level secondary data for 21 municipalities
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although this empirical multi-method study measures household water access, supply intermittency, and informal water market costs across small municipalities in Paraíba, Brazil (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6), its empirical exposure is generic water transfer infrastructure delivery (the São Francisco River Integration Project, PISF) and demographic, climatic, hydrological, and physical distribution factors within a DPSIR model (Table 1). It does not empirically examine a rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or institutional mechanism governing service access, referencing governance and planning only as unanalysed background and policy recommendations.
raw_response.study_design: Multi-method case study integrating repeated cross-sectional household surveys (2021 and 2024) with longitudinal secondary municipal geospatial, hydrological, and economic data within a DPSIR framework
